title: Digital Marketing for Dealer Principals and General Managers
description: What a dealer principal or GM needs from digital marketing: one page of numbers, vendors held to account, and the three leaks that cost the most gross.
h1: For dealer principals and GMs: know what's working.
why: You don't need to run the campaigns. You need to know which ones are working, and where the store is leaking.
intro: You're paying for a website, a CRM, ads, listings and probably an agency. Every one of them sends a report that says things are going well. Your job isn't to read those — it's to know, on one page, whether marketing is selling cars and where the store is losing them.
problems: Too many vendors, no single answer
Each vendor reports on its own piece. Nobody reports on sold units by source.
Reports you can't act on
Impressions and clicks don't hit a forecast. Appointments, shows and deliveries do.
Leads paid for, then lost
Slow follow-up quietly costs more gross than any ad problem.
No one owns digital
When it's everyone's job, it's nobody's.
numbers: Cost per sold unit, by source
Median minutes to first human reply
faqs: What should I ask my marketing vendors for?
One page a month: leads by source, response time, appointments, shows, sold units and cost per sold unit. If they can't produce it, that tells you something.
Where do most stores lose the most money?
Lead follow-up. It's usually the cheapest thing to fix and the biggest leak.
How involved do I need to be?
Fifteen minutes a month with the right page in front of you is enough.

title: Digital Marketing for Dealership Sales Managers
description: For GSMs and sales managers: turn internet leads into appointments with faster first replies, text-first follow-up and a process that survives a busy Saturday.
h1: For sales managers: turn leads into appointments.
why: Most of the gross lost online is lost after the lead arrives. These are about the handoff from screen to showroom.
intro: Marketing's job is to make the phone ring. Yours is what happens next. Most stores lose more deals between the lead and the appointment than anywhere else — not because the team doesn't care, but because the process breaks on a busy day.
problems: Leads sit while the floor is busy
Saturdays and evenings are when leads arrive and when nobody is free.
Generic first replies
"Thanks for your interest" gets ignored. A specific text about the exact vehicle gets answered.
No-shows
An appointment without a confirmation and a reason to come is a maybe.
Arguments about lead quality
Usually settled by measuring response time first.
faqs: How fast is fast enough?
A real person, by name, inside ten minutes during the hours your shoppers are shopping.
Should salespeople or a BDC handle leads?
Either works if one named person owns first response each shift. What fails is "whoever's free".
How do I prove it to the team?
Mystery shop your own store monthly and post the results.

title: Digital Marketing for Internet and BDC Managers
description: For internet and BDC managers: better vehicle pages, faster first replies, text-first follow-up and tracking that shows which leads turn into sales.
h1: For internet and BDC managers: more appointments from the same leads.
why: Your job is turning clicks into appointments. Start with the pages shoppers land on and the first reply they get.
intro: You sit between the website and the showroom. When vehicle pages are thin, you get fewer leads; when first replies are slow or generic, you set fewer appointments. Fixing those two ends is where your numbers move.
problems: Thin vehicle pages
Few photos, no price, no real description — fewer shoppers submit.
Slow pages on phones
Shoppers leave before they see the car.
One script for every lead
A specific reply about the exact vehicle beats any template.
No idea which source sells
Without tracking links, every channel looks the same.
faqs: Text or call first?
Text first, then call. A text waits until the shopper is ready.
How do I show which sources work?
Tag every link you control and make sure the CRM records source on every lead.
What's the quickest win?
Cut your lead form to name, contact method and vehicle.

title: Digital Marketing for Dealership Marketing Managers
description: For dealership marketing managers: local SEO, Google Business Profile, social and email habits that outperform most paid campaigns — and how to report on them.
h1: For marketing managers: build the habits that compound.
why: Local search, social and your own database do more than most paid campaigns. Build the habits first.
intro: You're usually a team of one, handling the website, social, email, events and three vendors. You can't do everything, so do the things that compound: a strong Google profile, steady real content and email to the customers you already have.
problems: Stretched across everything
The work that compounds — profile, reviews, email — gets squeezed out by urgent requests.
Stock content
Manufacturer creative looks like every other store's.
Hard to show results
Without tracking, good work is invisible to the GM.
Vendors who don't coordinate
Website, ads and social all saying different things.
numbers: Calls and direction requests from Google
faqs: Where should I spend my first hour each week?
Google Business Profile: one post, five photos, every review answered.
How do I get real content from the sales floor?
Agree simple rules once, then make it easy — one shared album, one person collecting on Fridays.
How do I report to the GM?
One page tied to appointments and sold units, not impressions.

title: Digital Marketing for Dealership Service Managers
description: For service managers: fill the bays with Google Business Profile, reviews, seasonal offers and a service-to-sales handoff that actually happens.
h1: For service managers: fill the bays and keep them coming back.
why: You see more customers than the sales floor. Your reviews and your lane drive repeat business for the whole store.
intro: Service touches more customers in a month than sales does in a quarter, and it's where loyalty is won or lost. Yet most dealership marketing ignores it. A few simple habits bring in more service work and feed sales at the same time.
problems: Service is invisible on Google
Wrong hours, no service phone number, no service photos.
Few service reviews
Sales gets asked; service doesn't.
Seasonal rushes handled late
Tire season offers go out after the first snow.
No handoff to sales
Good-equity customers leave without a conversation.
faqs: How do I get more service reviews?
Ask at pickup, by text with a direct link, every time.
Should service have its own Google listing?
At minimum, its own department hours and phone number. Sometimes a separate listing makes sense.
What should I post?
Seasonal offers and short tips, with real photos of your team and bays.

title: Digital Marketing for Used Car Managers
description: For used car managers: get units found, trusted and sold faster with better merchandising, local search and a day-30 review habit.
h1: For used car managers: turn inventory faster.
why: Every day a unit sits costs you. These are about getting used inventory found, trusted and sold faster.
intro: Two identical trades, priced the same: one sells in a week, one sits for two months. The difference is almost never the car. It's the photos, the description, the history report and whether the listing shows up when someone searches.
problems: Slow from trade to online
Every day in recon or waiting for photos is a day not for sale.
Thin listings
Few photos and option-code descriptions read as something to hide.
Reacting at day 60
By then the market has moved.
Matching every competitor
Giving up gross on deals that weren't leaving.
numbers: Days from trade to live listing
faqs: How many photos does a used unit need?
Twenty-five to forty, in the same order every time, including any flaws.
When should I reprice?
Review at day 30. If it has views but no leads, the listing or price is the issue.
Should I match a competitor's price?
Compare the two vehicles side by side first. Often the gap isn't real.
